The camera's subtle movement, following the water back into the ocean, creates a sense of fluidity, echoing the ebb and flow of Mara's thoughts.

She stops outside an abandoned fishing boat.

She touches the wood.

A memory flashes.

Her father laughing.

A storm.

His boat disappearing into darkness.

The memory ends.

project_5907c60cddbc.script_text:
I WAS REBORN
Short Film Script
Genre: Post-Apocalyptic Revenge Thriller / Psychological Drama
Setting: Downtown Chicago
LOGLINE
After being betrayed and killed by the people she trusted during the apocalypse, Maya
Carter wakes up two months before the collapse. Given a second life, she prepares a
hidden Chicago homestead, saves a chosen few, and must decide whether revenge or
rebuilding is the true purpose of being reborn.
OPENING
EXT. DOWNTOWN CHICAGO — GOLDEN HOUR
Chicago is alive. The L train moves through the skyline. People fill the streets. Music,
laughter, families, restaurants, Lake Michigan reflecting the sunset.
Maya walks through the city watching small moments people take for granted.
MAYA (V.O.)
People think the end of the world is fire. Buildings
falling. Chaos. But the hardest part is remembering
when it was beautiful.
CUT TO:
EXT. DOWNTOWN CHICAGO — AFTER THE APOCALYPSE
The same city. Different world. The L train is frozen. Buildings are cracked. Nature has
reclaimed the streets. The skyline still stands, but Chicago feels like a graveyard.
Maya walks through the ruins. She reaches the Chicago River. The place where she
died.
THE FIRST TIMELINE
Maya is surrounded by the people she trusted. Dre, her closest friend, stands among
them. His jaw is tight. He won't look her in the eyes.
DRE
I need you to understand something.MAYA
That's funny.
DRE
What?
MAYA
You always say that right before you do something
you know is wrong.
DRE
Things changed.
MAYA
No. People changed.
DRE
(raises the gun)
There's not enough. You have to understand that.
There is not enough for everyone.
MAYA
So you decided that for all of us.
DRE
Someone had to.
(pulls the trigger)
Maya is killed. Darkness.
We hold on Dre's face for a beat after the shot. He doesn't look relieved. He looks like
a man who just chose scarcity over trust — and already knows the cost.
THE SECOND CHANCE
Maya wakes up. Two months before the apocalypse. She remembers everything. The
betrayal. The death. The collapse.
She looks out at Chicago while it is still alive. The L train runs. People laugh below her
window.
MAYA
I remember dying. So why am I here?
She sits with that for a long moment. Then something shifts behind her eyes. Not grief.
Not rage. Clarity.
DRE — BEFORE THE FALL
INT. DRE'S APARTMENT — NIGHTMaya visits Dre. He doesn't know what she knows. To him, everything is still normal.
He's cooking. Music playing. The apartment feels lived-in, warm.
She watches him from the doorway before he notices her.
MAYA (V.O.)
This is the version of him I want to remember. The
one who used to split his last twenty dollars with me at
the gas station. The one who showed up when I
needed him. That person was real. I have to believe
that.
Dre turns and sees her.
DRE
You good? You're looking at me weird.
MAYA
I'm fine. Just tired.
DRE
You eat?
MAYA
Yeah.
He puts a plate in front of her anyway. She looks down at it. She knows that in two
months this apartment will be stripped bare. She knows what hunger will do to him.
MAYA
Hey. If something happened — something bad —
you'd tell me, right?
DRE
What kind of something?
MAYA
I don't know. Anything. Would you come to me?
DRE
(beat, easy smile)
Maya. You're my people. Always.
She nods. She almost believes him.
THE COUNTDOWN
Maya creates a survival blueprint. Food. Water. Power. Medical. Security. People.
She writes two lists.
The first list: names of people she will save.
The second list: names she cannot. Dre's name is not on either list yet.She stares at both lists for a long time. Then she folds them and puts them away.
THE HOMESTEAD
EXT./INT. ABANDONED HIGH RISE, DOWNTOWN CHICAGO — DAY
Maya finds an abandoned high rise in Downtown Chicago. A building everyone forgot.
She sees a future inside it. She transforms it into a survival sanctuary.
The rooftop becomes a farm. Hydroponics. Seeds. Rain collection. Winter preparation.
The building gets solar power, batteries, generators, storage rooms, a medical area,
security systems, and emergency exits.
MAYA (V.O.)
I'm not preparing for monsters. I'm preparing for
people. People are always the hardest part.
SUPPLIES
Maya collects supplies before the world knows it needs them. Food. Water filters.
Medicine. Tools. Seeds. Preservation equipment. Repair materials.
She learns how to maintain everything. Every decision matters because she knows
time is running out.
THE SUPPLY RUN — WHAT GOES WRONG
EXT. SOUTH SIDE WAREHOUSE DISTRICT — NIGHT
Maya is mid-run. She's loaded two carts of medical supplies from an overlooked
pharmaceutical warehouse. She's almost to the loading dock when she hears voices.
Three men. Armed. Not police. Scavengers — before the scavenging has even
officially started.
She freezes. One cart tips. A glass bottle shatters on the concrete floor.
The men look toward the sound.
Maya abandons one cart. She pushes the other into the dark and holds her breath
against a pillar while they sweep the room with flashlights.
She gets out. But she lost half the antibiotics she came for.
INT. THE HOMESTEAD — LATER
She sits on the floor. Looks at what she saved. Then at the list of what she lost.
MAYA
(to herself)
Not enough. It's never going to be enough.
She stays there for a moment. Then she gets back up. She writes a new list. Different
warehouses. Different approach. She adapts.THE CHOSEN — RECRUITMENT
INT. COOK COUNTY HOSPITAL — BREAK ROOM — DAY
SIMONE, 40s, a trauma nurse with twelve-hour circles under her eyes, is eating alone.
Maya sits across from her uninvited.
MAYA
You worked the West Side clinic flood response in '19.
SIMONE
(without looking up)
Do I know you?
MAYA
Not yet. I need someone who can work with almost
nothing and keep people alive.
SIMONE
That's my whole job.
MAYA
Then this should feel familiar.
Simone finally looks up. Something in Maya's tone cuts through the exhaustion.
EXT. SOUTH CHICAGO AUTO SHOP — DAY
JAY, 30s, Maya's cousin — quiet, meticulous — is mid-repair on an old generator. He's
the kind of person who fixes things not because he has to but because broken things
bother him.
Maya leans against the bay door.
MAYA
I need you to look at something.
JAY
Where?
MAYA
Building downtown. Off the grid.
JAY
What for?
MAYA
I need to know if the solar setup will hold through a
Chicago winter.
JAY
(wipes his hands on a rag)
What are you building, Maya?MAYA
Something that lasts.
He follows her.
INT. COMMUNITY GARDEN, PILSEN — DAY
ELENA, 60s, is tending rows of winter kale. She doesn't stop working when Maya
approaches.
ELENA
You the one who's been asking about hydroponics at
the library?
MAYA
Yes.
ELENA
You don't have soil. So you're growing indoors.
MAYA
Rooftop. Maybe indoors eventually.
ELENA
(still not looking up)
Why?
MAYA
Because I think the stores are going to stop.
Elena pauses. She looks at Maya for a long moment.
ELENA
You're not the first person to feel that.
MAYA
I might be the first one doing something about it.
Elena sets down her trowel.
MAYA AND HER MOM
INT. MOM'S APARTMENT, BRONZEVILLE — EVENING
Maya visits her mother. Her mother notices she is different.
MOM
What?
MAYA
Nothing.
MOM
You have been staring at me forever.MAYA
I just forgot what it felt like to see you.
Mom sets down her tea. She looks at her daughter.
MOM
Baby. What's going on with you?
MAYA
I need you to trust me about something.
MOM
I always trust you.
MAYA
Even if I can't explain it yet.
A long beat. Mom reaches across the table and covers Maya's hand with hers.
MOM
Where do you need me to go?
Maya exhales for the first time in weeks.
DRE NOTICES
INT. DRE'S APARTMENT — DAY
Dre notices Maya changing.
You don't trust me anymore.
I trust what people show me.

And what did I show you?
DRE
MAYA
DRE
MAYA
Enough.
DRE
(frustrated)
That's not an answer, Maya.
MAYA
It's the only one I have right now.
She leaves. Dre watches her go. Something is working behind his eyes — not
suspicion, not anger. Something closer to fear.
THE WEIGHT OF KNOWINGINT. THE HOMESTEAD — ROOFTOP — NIGHT
Maya is alone. The city is still lit below her. Chicago in its last weeks of normal.
She has Dre's address written on a piece of paper. She's been carrying it for days. She
could warn him. She could bring him in. She could also make sure he never has the
chance to do what he did.
MAYA (V.O.)
I thought about it. I won't pretend I didn't. Every
version of what I could do to him before he did it to
me. And I understood — that feeling. I understood Dre
more in that moment than I ever had.
She stands at the roof's edge. City lights below.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
That's what scarcity does. It makes the math feel
simple. It makes monsters feel like realists. And I was
standing right at the edge of the same math.
She crumples the paper. She doesn't throw it away. She puts it back in her pocket.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
I put it away because I realized — I wasn't given this
second life to become what killed me. I was given it to
prove there was another way.
THE LAST NORMAL DAYS
EXT. CHICAGO — VARIOUS LOCATIONS — DAY
Chicago is still beautiful. People celebrate. People laugh. Maya moves through it all
like she's memorizing it. Every storefront. Every face. Every ordinary miracle.
MAYA (V.O.)
People ask what you'd do differently if you knew. I
know now. You'd stop skipping the small things. You'd
stay at the table longer.
THE APOCALYPSE BEGINS
The first blackout happens. Then another. The city changes. The hospitals collapse.
The streets become dangerous. Stores empty. People fight for resources. Chicago
becomes unrecognizable.
But Maya's homestead works. The building comes alive. Her preparation becomes
reality.
The cause: a cascading infrastructure failure — power grid, then supply chains, then
communications. Not one event. A system that was already failing, finally failing all at
once.THE HOMESTEAD COMMUNITY
INT. THE HOMESTEAD — VARIOUS — DAY
Inside are Maya's chosen survivors. Her mother. Jay. Simone. Elena. Others she
trusted. The building has food. Water. Power. Life.
Simone runs the medical floor. Jay keeps the power on. Elena tends the rooftop farm.
Maya's mother moves through all of it — feeding people, keeping rhythm, being the
warmth the building needs.
Outside, the city continues falling apart.
A MEAL SAVED FOR
INT. MAYA'S KITCHEN — EVENING
Late light through a thin curtain. A single pot of water works toward a boil. On the
counter: a small, careful inventory — spaghetti, a few fillets of catfish, one tomato,
garlic going soft at the root. Portions stretched carefully to reach four.
Mom stands at the stove, sleeves pushed up. Maya leans in the doorway a beat before
she moves — watching before joining, the way she does.
MOM
(not turning around)
You gonna help, or you gonna haunt the doorway all
night.
Maya smiles despite herself. Crosses in. Picks up the garlic without being asked.
Close on hands: Maya peeling garlic, the papery skin coming away in small curls. Mom
salting the water — a practiced toss, more feel than measurement.
MAYA
We're really doing the catfish? For all of us?
MOM
Been saving it. Tonight's a good night for it.
A beat. Maya doesn't ask why tonight. She understands it without needing to.
Mom sets up her station with quiet ritual — a shallow dish of cornmeal and flour,
seasoned heavy; a bowl of buttermilk gone slightly warm; a deep, heavy pot with oil
creeping up its sides. She drags a fingertip through the oil's surface, waits, watches for
the shimmer.
The catfish fillets soak in the buttermilk — Mom turning each one over with her fingers,
coating them fully. One by one, she lifts them dripping and presses them into the
cornmeal, turning, pressing again, making sure every edge is caught.
Maya drops the spaghetti into the boiling pot — more of it than usual, enough to
matter. Stirs. The kitchen fills with steam from her side and, from Mom's, the low tick
and pop of oil coming up to heat.Mom tests the oil with a pinch of cornmeal flicked in — it sizzles and rises
immediately. Satisfied, she lowers the first fillet in with careful hands, then the next,
then the next. The oil roars up around them, a wall of sound and rising gold bubbles.
A long moment with no dialogue. Just: the churn of frying oil. The soft roll of boiling
water. Wooden spoon against metal. Golden evening light thickening to amber across
the counter, catching the steam and the oil's haze like it's lit from within.
Mom watches the fillets with total attention now — nudging them gently so they don't
stick to the bottom, listening for the sound to change, the color to deepen. She lifts
one at the edge with a slotted spoon, checks the color, lowers it back.
Maya watches her mother's hands — the sureness of them, built from doing this with
less than they needed, and now stretching it further still.
MAYA
(quiet)
It smells like it used to.
Mom glances at her — just a flicker, something tender and unspoken passing between
them. She doesn't look away from the pot for long.
One by one, she lifts the fillets out, deep gold and crackling, onto a plate lined with
paper towel. The oil hisses and settles as each one comes free.
MOM
Taste this.
She tears a small corner off one fillet, blows on it, hands it to Maya. Maya takes it,
bites, and for a second just chews — eyes closing, something like relief crossing her
face.
MAYA
Perfect.
MOM
(small, satisfied)
Course it is.
They plate the food together — four bowls of spaghetti, a piece of crackling catfish laid
across each, careful that no one's portion looks smaller than another's.
They carry the bowls out toward the others — Jay, Elena, Simone waiting, low light
catching the steam rising off four plates instead of two.
Bowls set down one by one. No ceremony, just the quiet efficiency of people who've
learned to move around each other in small spaces. Maya hands Jay his plate; Elena
scoots over to make room; Simone's already reaching for a fork before hers even
lands.
For a moment, no one eats. Everyone around a table built for fewer — Mom the last to
sit, wiping her hands on her apron before finally lowering into her chair.A beat of stillness. Steam curling upward, catching the last of the amber light.
Then, without a word, they all start at once — the small clatter of forks, the first bite.
Jay closes his eyes over the fish the way Maya did earlier. He says something too
quiet to hear, and Elena laughs, soft and real.
Mom watches them eat before touching her own plate — the same look she gave
Maya earlier, multiplied across the table.
Hold on the group — heads bent over their bowls, the room lit gold, the ones who
made it this far, eating like it's nothing and like it's everything.
FINAL CONFRONTATION
EXT./INT. THE HOMESTEAD — DAY
Dre finds the building. He looks rough — hollowed out, hungry. But his eyes are still
sharp. He sees everything.
The lights. The gardens. The survivors. He sees Maya's mother alive through a
window.
He understands she knew.
DRE
How?
Maya says nothing.
DRE
How did you know?
MAYA
I had a nightmare.
DRE
A nightmare.
MAYA
The kind you wake up from different.
DRE
(quiet, not accusatory — just broken)
You could have saved us.
MAYA
I tried.
DRE
When?
MAYA
Before you became the person who needed saving.A long silence. Dre looks at the building — the life inside it. Then back at Maya.
DRE
(barely)
scared.
I was scared. I want you to know that. I was so
MAYA
I know.
DRE
Does it matter?
MAYA
(beat)
It matters that you said it.
Maya gives Dre supplies. A map. A chance. But not her sanctuary. Not her future. She
watches him go. She doesn't look away until he's gone.
ENDING
EXT. THE HOMESTEAD — ROOFTOP — DUSK
Maya stands on the rooftop. Chicago is dark. Her building glows. Plants move in the
wind. A small piece of humanity survives.
Below, she can hear voices. Her mother. Jay. Simone. Elena. People living.
MAYA (V.O.)
The first time the world ended, I lost everything.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The second time, I prepared.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
I thought being reborn meant getting revenge. I was
wrong.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
It meant I finally had the power to choose what
survived.
She looks out at the dark city. At the stars finally visible without the light pollution.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The nightmare showed me who we became. The
second chance showed me who we could be instead.
I chose that version. Every single day, I chose it.
FADE TO BLACK.FADE OUT.

scenes.heading: INT. MAYA'S KITCHEN — EVENING
scenes.text:
Late light through a thin curtain. A single pot of water works toward a boil. On the
counter: a small, careful inventory — spaghetti, a few fillets of catfish, one tomato,
garlic going soft at the root. Portions stretched carefully to reach four.
Mom stands at the stove, sleeves pushed up. Maya leans in the doorway a beat before
she moves — watching before joining, the way she does.
MOM
(not turning around)
You gonna help, or you gonna haunt the doorway all
night.
Maya smiles despite herself. Crosses in. Picks up the garlic without being asked.
Close on hands: Maya peeling garlic, the papery skin coming away in small curls. Mom
salting the water — a practiced toss, more feel than measurement.
MAYA
We're really doing the catfish? For all of us?
MOM
Been saving it. Tonight's a good night for it.
A beat. Maya doesn't ask why tonight. She understands it without needing to.
Mom sets up her station with quiet ritual — a shallow dish of cornmeal and flour,
seasoned heavy; a bowl of buttermilk gone slightly warm; a deep, heavy pot with oil
creeping up its sides. She drags a fingertip through the oil's surface, waits, watches for
the shimmer.
The catfish fillets soak in the buttermilk — Mom turning each one over with her fingers,
coating them fully. One by one, she lifts them dripping and presses them into the
cornmeal, turning, pressing again, making sure every edge is caught.
Maya drops the spaghetti into the boiling pot — more of it than usual, enough to
matter. Stirs. The kitchen fills with steam from her side and, from Mom's, the low tick
and pop of oil coming up to heat.Mom tests the oil with a pinch of cornmeal flicked in — it sizzles and rises
immediately. Satisfied, she lowers the first fillet in with careful hands, then the next,
then the next. The oil roars up around them, a wall of sound and rising gold bubbles.
A long moment with no dialogue. Just: the churn of frying oil. The soft roll of boiling
water. Wooden spoon against metal. Golden evening light thickening to amber across
the counter, catching the steam and the oil's haze like it's lit from within.
Mom watches the fillets with total attention now — nudging them gently so they don't
stick to the bottom, listening for the sound to change, the color to deepen. She lifts
one at the edge with a slotted spoon, checks the color, lowers it back.
Maya watches her mother's hands — the sureness of them, built from doing this with
less than they needed, and now stretching it further still.
MAYA
(quiet)
It smells like it used to.
Mom glances at her — just a flicker, something tender and unspoken passing between
them. She doesn't look away from the pot for long.
One by one, she lifts the fillets out, deep gold and crackling, onto a plate lined with
paper towel. The oil hisses and settles as each one comes free.
MOM
Taste this.
She tears a small corner off one fillet, blows on it, hands it to Maya. Maya takes it,
bites, and for a second just chews — eyes closing, something like relief crossing her
face.
MAYA
Perfect.
MOM
(small, satisfied)
Course it is.
They plate the food together — four bowls of spaghetti, a piece of crackling catfish laid
across each, careful that no one's portion looks smaller than another's.
They carry the bowls out toward the others — Jay, Elena, Simone waiting, low light
catching the steam rising off four plates instead of two.
Bowls set down one by one. No ceremony, just the quiet efficiency of people who've
learned to move around each other in small spaces. Maya hands Jay his plate; Elena
scoots over to make room; Simone's already reaching for a fork before hers even
lands.
For a moment, no one eats. Everyone around a table built for fewer — Mom the last to
sit, wiping her hands on her apron before finally lowering into her chair.A beat of stillness. Steam curling upward, catching the last of the amber light.
Then, without a word, they all start at once — the small clatter of forks, the first bite.
Jay closes his eyes over the fish the way Maya did earlier. He says something too
quiet to hear, and Elena laughs, soft and real.
Mom watches them eat before touching her own plate — the same look she gave
Maya earlier, multiplied across the table.
Hold on the group — heads bent over their bowls, the room lit gold, the ones who
made it this far, eating like it's nothing and like it's everything.
FINAL CONFRONTATION
EXT./INT. THE HOMESTEAD — DAY
Dre finds the building. He looks rough — hollowed out, hungry. But his eyes are still
sharp. He sees everything.
The lights. The gardens. The survivors. He sees Maya's mother alive through a
window.
He understands she knew.
DRE
How?
Maya says nothing.
DRE
How did you know?
MAYA
I had a nightmare.
DRE
A nightmare.
MAYA
The kind you wake up from different.
DRE
(quiet, not accusatory — just broken)
You could have saved us.
MAYA
I tried.
DRE
When?
MAYA
Before you became the person who needed saving.A long silence. Dre looks at the building — the life inside it. Then back at Maya.
DRE
(barely)
scared.
I was scared. I want you to know that. I was so
MAYA
I know.
DRE
Does it matter?
MAYA
(beat)
It matters that you said it.
Maya gives Dre supplies. A map. A chance. But not her sanctuary. Not her future. She
watches him go. She doesn't look away until he's gone.
ENDING

scenes.heading: EXT. THE HOMESTEAD — ROOFTOP — DUSK
scenes.text:
Maya stands on the rooftop. Chicago is dark. Her building glows. Plants move in the
wind. A small piece of humanity survives.
Below, she can hear voices. Her mother. Jay. Simone. Elena. People living.
MAYA (V.O.)
The first time the world ended, I lost everything.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The second time, I prepared.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
I thought being reborn meant getting revenge. I was
wrong.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
It meant I finally had the power to choose what
survived.
She looks out at the dark city. At the stars finally visible without the light pollution.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The nightmare showed me who we became. The
second chance showed me who we could be instead.
I chose that version. Every single day, I chose it.
FADE TO BLACK.FADE OUT.

scene_001.heading: EXT. DOWNTOWN CHICAGO — GOLDEN HOUR
scene_001.text:
Chicago is alive. The L train moves through the skyline. People fill the streets. Music,
laughter, families, restaurants, Lake Michigan reflecting the sunset.
Maya walks through the city watching small moments people take for granted.
MAYA (V.O.)
People think the end of the world is fire. Buildings
falling. Chaos. But the hardest part is remembering
when it was beautiful.
CUT TO:

scene_002.heading: EXT. DOWNTOWN CHICAGO — AFTER THE APOCALYPSE
scene_002.text:
The same city. Different world. The L train is frozen. Buildings are cracked. Nature has
reclaimed the streets. The skyline still stands, but Chicago feels like a graveyard.
Maya walks through the ruins. She reaches the Chicago River. The place where she
died.
THE FIRST TIMELINE
Maya is surrounded by the people she trusted. Dre, her closest friend, stands among
them. His jaw is tight. He won't look her in the eyes.
DRE
I need you to understand something.MAYA
That's funny.
DRE
What?
MAYA
You always say that right before you do something
you know is wrong.
DRE
Things changed.
MAYA
No. People changed.
DRE
(raises the gun)
There's not enough. You have to understand that.
There is not enough for everyone.
MAYA
So you decided that for all of us.
DRE
Someone had to.
(pulls the trigger)
Maya is killed. Darkness.
We hold on Dre's face for a beat after the shot. He doesn't look relieved. He looks like
a man who just chose scarcity over trust — and already knows the cost.
THE SECOND CHANCE
Maya wakes up. Two months before the apocalypse. She remembers everything. The
betrayal. The death. The collapse.
She looks out at Chicago while it is still alive. The L train runs. People laugh below her
window.
MAYA
I remember dying. So why am I here?
She sits with that for a long moment. Then something shifts behind her eyes. Not grief.
Not rage. Clarity.
DRE — BEFORE THE FALL

scene_003.heading: INT. DRE'S APARTMENT — NIGHTMaya visits Dre. He doesn't know what she knows. To him, everything is still normal.
scene_003.location: DRE'S APARTMENT — NIGHTMaya visits Dre. He doesn't know what she knows. To him, everything is still normal.
scene_003.text:
He's cooking. Music playing. The apartment feels lived-in, warm.
She watches him from the doorway before he notices her.
MAYA (V.O.)
This is the version of him I want to remember. The
one who used to split his last twenty dollars with me at
the gas station. The one who showed up when I
needed him. That person was real. I have to believe
that.
Dre turns and sees her.
DRE
You good? You're looking at me weird.
MAYA
I'm fine. Just tired.
DRE
You eat?
MAYA
Yeah.
He puts a plate in front of her anyway. She looks down at it. She knows that in two
months this apartment will be stripped bare. She knows what hunger will do to him.
MAYA
Hey. If something happened — something bad —
you'd tell me, right?
DRE
What kind of something?
MAYA
I don't know. Anything. Would you come to me?
DRE
(beat, easy smile)
Maya. You're my people. Always.
She nods. She almost believes him.
THE COUNTDOWN
Maya creates a survival blueprint. Food. Water. Power. Medical. Security. People.
She writes two lists.
The first list: names of people she will save.
The second list: names she cannot. Dre's name is not on either list yet.She stares at both lists for a long time. Then she folds them and puts them away.
THE HOMESTEAD
EXT./INT. ABANDONED HIGH RISE, DOWNTOWN CHICAGO — DAY
Maya finds an abandoned high rise in Downtown Chicago. A building everyone forgot.
She sees a future inside it. She transforms it into a survival sanctuary.
The rooftop becomes a farm. Hydroponics. Seeds. Rain collection. Winter preparation.
The building gets solar power, batteries, generators, storage rooms, a medical area,
security systems, and emergency exits.
MAYA (V.O.)
I'm not preparing for monsters. I'm preparing for
people. People are always the hardest part.
SUPPLIES
Maya collects supplies before the world knows it needs them. Food. Water filters.
Medicine. Tools. Seeds. Preservation equipment. Repair materials.
She learns how to maintain everything. Every decision matters because she knows
time is running out.
THE SUPPLY RUN — WHAT GOES WRONG

scene_004.heading: EXT. SOUTH SIDE WAREHOUSE DISTRICT — NIGHT
scene_004.text:
Maya is mid-run. She's loaded two carts of medical supplies from an overlooked
pharmaceutical warehouse. She's almost to the loading dock when she hears voices.
Three men. Armed. Not police. Scavengers — before the scavenging has even
officially started.
She freezes. One cart tips. A glass bottle shatters on the concrete floor.
The men look toward the sound.
Maya abandons one cart. She pushes the other into the dark and holds her breath
against a pillar while they sweep the room with flashlights.
She gets out. But she lost half the antibiotics she came for.

scene_005.text:
She sits on the floor. Looks at what she saved. Then at the list of what she lost.
MAYA
(to herself)
Not enough. It's never going to be enough.
She stays there for a moment. Then she gets back up. She writes a new list. Different
warehouses. Different approach. She adapts.THE CHOSEN — RECRUITMENT

scene_006.heading: INT. COOK COUNTY HOSPITAL — BREAK ROOM — DAY
scene_006.location: COOK COUNTY HOSPITAL — BREAK ROOM — DAY
scene_006.text:
SIMONE, 40s, a trauma nurse with twelve-hour circles under her eyes, is eating alone.
Maya sits across from her uninvited.
MAYA
You worked the West Side clinic flood response in '19.
SIMONE
(without looking up)
Do I know you?
MAYA
Not yet. I need someone who can work with almost
nothing and keep people alive.
SIMONE
That's my whole job.
MAYA
Then this should feel familiar.
Simone finally looks up. Something in Maya's tone cuts through the exhaustion.

scene_007.heading: EXT. SOUTH CHICAGO AUTO SHOP — DAY
scene_007.text:
JAY, 30s, Maya's cousin — quiet, meticulous — is mid-repair on an old generator. He's
the kind of person who fixes things not because he has to but because broken things
bother him.
Maya leans against the bay door.
MAYA
I need you to look at something.
JAY
Where?
MAYA
Building downtown. Off the grid.
JAY
What for?
MAYA
I need to know if the solar setup will hold through a
Chicago winter.
JAY
(wipes his hands on a rag)
What are you building, Maya?MAYA
Something that lasts.
He follows her.

scene_008.heading: INT. COMMUNITY GARDEN, PILSEN — DAY
scene_008.text:
ELENA, 60s, is tending rows of winter kale. She doesn't stop working when Maya
approaches.
ELENA
You the one who's been asking about hydroponics at
the library?
MAYA
Yes.
ELENA
You don't have soil. So you're growing indoors.
MAYA
Rooftop. Maybe indoors eventually.
ELENA

scene_011.text:
Chicago is still beautiful. People celebrate. People laugh. Maya moves through it all
like she's memorizing it. Every storefront. Every face. Every ordinary miracle.

know now. You'd stop skipping the small things. You'd
stay at the table longer.

The streets become dangerous. Stores empty. People fight for resources. Chicago
becomes unrecognizable.

reality.

communications. Not one event. A system that was already failing, finally failing all at
once.THE HOMESTEAD COMMUNITY

scene_013.heading: INT. MAYA'S KITCHEN — EVENING
scene_013.text:
Late light through a thin curtain. A single pot of water works toward a boil. On the
counter: a small, careful inventory — spaghetti, a few fillets of catfish, one tomato,
garlic going soft at the root. Portions stretched carefully to reach four.
Mom stands at the stove, sleeves pushed up. Maya leans in the doorway a beat before
she moves — watching before joining, the way she does.
MOM
(not turning around)
You gonna help, or you gonna haunt the doorway all
night.
Maya smiles despite herself. Crosses in. Picks up the garlic without being asked.
Close on hands: Maya peeling garlic, the papery skin coming away in small curls. Mom
salting the water — a practiced toss, more feel than measurement.
MAYA
We're really doing the catfish? For all of us?
MOM
Been saving it. Tonight's a good night for it.
A beat. Maya doesn't ask why tonight. She understands it without needing to.
Mom sets up her station with quiet ritual — a shallow dish of cornmeal and flour,
seasoned heavy; a bowl of buttermilk gone slightly warm; a deep, heavy pot with oil
creeping up its sides. She drags a fingertip through the oil's surface, waits, watches for
the shimmer.
The catfish fillets soak in the buttermilk — Mom turning each one over with her fingers,
coating them fully. One by one, she lifts them dripping and presses them into the
cornmeal, turning, pressing again, making sure every edge is caught.
Maya drops the spaghetti into the boiling pot — more of it than usual, enough to
matter. Stirs. The kitchen fills with steam from her side and, from Mom's, the low tick
and pop of oil coming up to heat.Mom tests the oil with a pinch of cornmeal flicked in — it sizzles and rises
immediately. Satisfied, she lowers the first fillet in with careful hands, then the next,
then the next. The oil roars up around them, a wall of sound and rising gold bubbles.
A long moment with no dialogue. Just: the churn of frying oil. The soft roll of boiling
water. Wooden spoon against metal. Golden evening light thickening to amber across
the counter, catching the steam and the oil's haze like it's lit from within.
Mom watches the fillets with total attention now — nudging them gently so they don't
stick to the bottom, listening for the sound to change, the color to deepen. She lifts
one at the edge with a slotted spoon, checks the color, lowers it back.
Maya watches her mother's hands — the sureness of them, built from doing this with
less than they needed, and now stretching it further still.
MAYA
(quiet)
It smells like it used to.
Mom glances at her — just a flicker, something tender and unspoken passing between
them. She doesn't look away from the pot for long.
One by one, she lifts the fillets out, deep gold and crackling, onto a plate lined with
paper towel. The oil hisses and settles as each one comes free.
MOM
Taste this.
She tears a small corner off one fillet, blows on it, hands it to Maya. Maya takes it,
bites, and for a second just chews — eyes closing, something like relief crossing her
face.
MAYA
Perfect.
MOM
(small, satisfied)
Course it is.
They plate the food together — four bowls of spaghetti, a piece of crackling catfish laid
across each, careful that no one's portion looks smaller than another's.
They carry the bowls out toward the others — Jay, Elena, Simone waiting, low light
catching the steam rising off four plates instead of two.
Bowls set down one by one. No ceremony, just the quiet efficiency of people who've
learned to move around each other in small spaces. Maya hands Jay his plate; Elena
scoots over to make room; Simone's already reaching for a fork before hers even
lands.
For a moment, no one eats. Everyone around a table built for fewer — Mom the last to
sit, wiping her hands on her apron before finally lowering into her chair.A beat of stillness. Steam curling upward, catching the last of the amber light.
Then, without a word, they all start at once — the small clatter of forks, the first bite.
Jay closes his eyes over the fish the way Maya did earlier. He says something too
quiet to hear, and Elena laughs, soft and real.
Mom watches them eat before touching her own plate — the same look she gave
Maya earlier, multiplied across the table.
Hold on the group — heads bent over their bowls, the room lit gold, the ones who
made it this far, eating like it's nothing and like it's everything.
FINAL CONFRONTATION
EXT./INT. THE HOMESTEAD — DAY
Dre finds the building. He looks rough — hollowed out, hungry. But his eyes are still
sharp. He sees everything.
The lights. The gardens. The survivors. He sees Maya's mother alive through a
window.
He understands she knew.
DRE
How?
Maya says nothing.
DRE
How did you know?
MAYA
I had a nightmare.
DRE
A nightmare.
MAYA
The kind you wake up from different.
DRE
(quiet, not accusatory — just broken)
You could have saved us.
MAYA
I tried.
DRE
When?
MAYA
Before you became the person who needed saving.A long silence. Dre looks at the building — the life inside it. Then back at Maya.
DRE
(barely)
scared.
I was scared. I want you to know that. I was so
MAYA
I know.
DRE
Does it matter?
MAYA
(beat)
It matters that you said it.
Maya gives Dre supplies. A map. A chance. But not her sanctuary. Not her future. She
watches him go. She doesn't look away until he's gone.
ENDING

scene_014.heading: EXT. THE HOMESTEAD — ROOFTOP — DUSK
scene_014.text:
Maya stands on the rooftop. Chicago is dark. Her building glows. Plants move in the
wind. A small piece of humanity survives.
Below, she can hear voices. Her mother. Jay. Simone. Elena. People living.
MAYA (V.O.)
The first time the world ended, I lost everything.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The second time, I prepared.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
I thought being reborn meant getting revenge. I was
wrong.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
It meant I finally had the power to choose what
survived.
She looks out at the dark city. At the stars finally visible without the light pollution.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The nightmare showed me who we became. The
second chance showed me who we could be instead.
I chose that version. Every single day, I chose it.
FADE TO BLACK.FADE OUT.

previs_scene_board.intent:
Chicago is alive. The L train moves through the skyline. People fill the streets. Music,
laughter, families, restaurants, Lake Michigan reflecting the sunset.
Maya walks through the city watching small moments people take for granted.
MAYA (V.O.)
People think the end of the world is fire. Buildings
falling. Chaos. But the hardest part is remembering
when it was beautiful.
CUT TO:

The same city. Different world. The L train is frozen. Buildings are cracked. Nature has
reclaimed the streets. The skyline still stands, but Chicago feels like a graveyard.
Maya walks through the ruins. She reaches the Chicago River. The place where she
died.
THE FIRST TIMELINE
Maya is surrounded by the people she trusted. Dre, her closest friend, stands among
them. His jaw is tight. He won't look her in the eyes.
DRE
I need you to understand something.MAYA
That's funny.
DRE
What?
MAYA
You always say that right before you do something
you know is wrong.
DRE
Things changed.
MAYA
No. People changed.
DRE
(raises the gun)
There's not enough. You have to understand that.
There is not enough for everyone.
MAYA
So you decided that for all of us.
DRE
Someone had to.
(pulls the trigger)
Maya is killed. Darkness.
We hold on Dre's face for a beat after the shot. He doesn't look relieved. He looks like
a man who just chose scarcity over trust — and already knows the cost.
THE SECOND CHANCE
Maya wakes up. Two months before the apocalypse. She remembers everything. The
betrayal. The death. The collapse.
She looks out at Chicago while it is still alive. The L train runs. People laugh below her
window.
MAYA
I remember dying. So why am I here?
She sits with that for a long moment. Then something shifts behind her eyes. Not grief.
Not rage. Clarity.
DRE — BEFORE THE FALL

He's cooking. Music playing. The apartment feels lived-in, warm.
She watches him from the doorway before he notices her.
MAYA (V.O.)
This is the version of him I want to remember. The
one who used to split his last twenty dollars with me at
the gas station. The one who showed up when I
needed him. That person was real. I have to believe
that.
Dre turns and sees her.
DRE
You good? You're looking at me weird.
MAYA
I'm fine. Just tired.
DRE
You eat?
MAYA
Yeah.
He puts a plate in front of her anyway. She looks down at it. She knows that in two
months this apartment will be stripped bare. She knows what hunger will do to him.
MAYA
Hey. If something happened — something bad —
you'd tell me, right?
DRE
What kind of something?
MAYA
I don't know. Anything. Would you come to me?
DRE
(beat, easy smile)
Maya. You're my people. Always.
She nods. She almost believes him.
THE COUNTDOWN
Maya creates a survival blueprint. Food. Water. Power. Medical. Security. People.
She writes two lists.
The first list: names of people she will save.
The second list: names she cannot. Dre's name is not on either list yet.She stares at both lists for a long time. Then she folds them and puts them away.
THE HOMESTEAD
EXT./INT. ABANDONED HIGH RISE, DOWNTOWN CHICAGO — DAY
Maya finds an abandoned high rise in Downtown Chicago. A building everyone forgot.
She sees a future inside it. She transforms it into a survival sanctuary.
The rooftop becomes a farm. Hydroponics. Seeds. Rain collection. Winter preparation.
The building gets solar power, batteries, generators, storage rooms, a medical area,
security systems, and emergency exits.
MAYA (V.O.)
I'm not preparing for monsters. I'm preparing for
people. People are always the hardest part.
SUPPLIES
Maya collects supplies before the world knows it needs them. Food. Water filters.
Medicine. Tools. Seeds. Preservation equipment. Repair materials.
She learns how to maintain everything. Every decision matters because she knows
time is running out.
THE SUPPLY RUN — WHAT GOES WRONG

Maya is mid-run. She's loaded two carts of medical supplies from an overlooked
pharmaceutical warehouse. She's almost to the loading dock when she hears voices.
Three men. Armed. Not police. Scavengers — before the scavenging has even
officially started.
She freezes. One cart tips. A glass bottle shatters on the concrete floor.
The men look toward the sound.
Maya abandons one cart. She pushes the other into the dark and holds her breath
against a pillar while they sweep the room with flashlights.
She gets out. But she lost half the antibiotics she came for.

She sits on the floor. Looks at what she saved. Then at the list of what she lost.
MAYA
(to herself)
Not enough. It's never going to be enough.
She stays there for a moment. Then she gets back up. She writes a new list. Different
warehouses. Different approach. She adapts.THE CHOSEN — RECRUITMENT

SIMONE, 40s, a trauma nurse with twelve-hour circles under her eyes, is eating alone.
Maya sits across from her uninvited.
MAYA
You worked the West Side clinic flood response in '19.
SIMONE
(without looking up)
Do I know you?
MAYA
Not yet. I need someone who can work with almost
nothing and keep people alive.
SIMONE
That's my whole job.
MAYA
Then this should feel familiar.
Simone finally looks up. Something in Maya's tone cuts through the exhaustion.

JAY, 30s, Maya's cousin — quiet, meticulous — is mid-repair on an old generator. He's
the kind of person who fixes things not because he has to but because broken things
bother him.
Maya leans against the bay door.
MAYA
I need you to look at something.
JAY
Where?
MAYA
Building downtown. Off the grid.
JAY
What for?
MAYA
I need to know if the solar setup will hold through a
Chicago winter.
JAY
(wipes his hands on a rag)
What are you building, Maya?MAYA
Something that lasts.
He follows her.

ELENA, 60s, is tending rows of winter kale. She doesn't stop working when Maya
approaches.
ELENA
You the one who's been asking about hydroponics at
the library?
MAYA
Yes.
ELENA
You don't have soil. So you're growing indoors.
MAYA
Rooftop. Maybe indoors eventually.
ELENA
(still not looking up)
Why?
MAYA
Because I think the stores are going to stop.
Elena pauses. She looks at Maya for a long moment.
ELENA
You're not the first person to feel that.
MAYA
I might be the first one doing something about it.
Elena sets down her trowel.
MAYA AND HER MOM

Maya visits her mother. Her mother notices she is different.
MOM
What?
MAYA
Nothing.
MOM
You have been staring at me forever.MAYA
I just forgot what it felt like to see you.
Mom sets down her tea. She looks at her daughter.
MOM
Baby. What's going on with you?
MAYA
I need you to trust me about something.
MOM
I always trust you.
MAYA
Even if I can't explain it yet.
A long beat. Mom reaches across the table and covers Maya's hand with hers.
MOM
Where do you need me to go?
Maya exhales for the first time in weeks.
DRE NOTICES

Dre notices Maya changing.
You don't trust me anymore.
I trust what people show me.

And what did I show you?
DRE
MAYA
DRE
MAYA
Enough.
DRE
(frustrated)
That's not an answer, Maya.
MAYA
It's the only one I have right now.
She leaves. Dre watches her go. Something is working behind his eyes — not
suspicion, not anger. Something closer to fear.
THE WEIGHT OF KNOWINGINT. THE HOMESTEAD — ROOFTOP — NIGHT
Maya is alone. The city is still lit below her. Chicago in its last weeks of normal.
She has Dre's address written on a piece of paper. She's been carrying it for days. She
could warn him. She could bring him in. She could also make sure he never has the
chance to do what he did.
MAYA (V.O.)
I thought about it. I won't pretend I didn't. Every
version of what I could do to him before he did it to
me. And I understood — that feeling. I understood Dre
more in that moment than I ever had.
She stands at the roof's edge. City lights below.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
That's what scarcity does. It makes the math feel
simple. It makes monsters feel like realists. And I was
standing right at the edge of the same math.
She crumples the paper. She doesn't throw it away. She puts it back in her pocket.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
I put it away because I realized — I wasn't given this
second life to become what killed me. I was given it to
prove there was another way.
THE LAST NORMAL DAYS

Chicago is still beautiful. People celebrate. People laugh. Maya moves through it all
like she's memorizing it. Every storefront. Every face. Every ordinary miracle.
MAYA (V.O.)
People ask what you'd do differently if you knew. I
know now. You'd stop skipping the small things. You'd
stay at the table longer.
THE APOCALYPSE BEGINS
The first blackout happens. Then another. The city changes. The hospitals collapse.
The streets become dangerous. Stores empty. People fight for resources. Chicago
becomes unrecognizable.
But Maya's homestead works. The building comes alive. Her preparation becomes
reality.
The cause: a cascading infrastructure failure — power grid, then supply chains, then
communications. Not one event. A system that was already failing, finally failing all at
once.THE HOMESTEAD COMMUNITY

Inside are Maya's chosen survivors. Her mother. Jay. Simone. Elena. Others she
trusted. The building has food. Water. Power. Life.
Simone runs the medical floor. Jay keeps the power on. Elena tends the rooftop farm.
Maya's mother moves through all of it — feeding people, keeping rhythm, being the
warmth the building needs.
Outside, the city continues falling apart.
A MEAL SAVED FOR

Late light through a thin curtain. A single pot of water works toward a boil. On the
counter: a small, careful inventory — spaghetti, a few fillets of catfish, one tomato,
garlic going soft at the root. Portions stretched carefully to reach four.
Mom stands at the stove, sleeves pushed up. Maya leans in the doorway a beat before
she moves — watching before joining, the way she does.
MOM
(not turning around)
You gonna help, or you gonna haunt the doorway all
night.
Maya smiles despite herself. Crosses in. Picks up the garlic without being asked.
Close on hands: Maya peeling garlic, the papery skin coming away in small curls. Mom
salting the water — a practiced toss, more feel than measurement.
MAYA
We're really doing the catfish? For all of us?
MOM
Been saving it. Tonight's a good night for it.
A beat. Maya doesn't ask why tonight. She understands it without needing to.
Mom sets up her station with quiet ritual — a shallow dish of cornmeal and flour,
seasoned heavy; a bowl of buttermilk gone slightly warm; a deep, heavy pot with oil
creeping up its sides. She drags a fingertip through the oil's surface, waits, watches for
the shimmer.
The catfish fillets soak in the buttermilk — Mom turning each one over with her fingers,
coating them fully. One by one, she lifts them dripping and presses them into the
cornmeal, turning, pressing again, making sure every edge is caught.
Maya drops the spaghetti into the boiling pot — more of it than usual, enough to
matter. Stirs. The kitchen fills with steam from her side and, from Mom's, the low tick
and pop of oil coming up to heat.Mom tests the oil with a pinch of cornmeal flicked in — it sizzles and rises
immediately. Satisfied, she lowers the first fillet in with careful hands, then the next,
then the next. The oil roars up around them, a wall of sound and rising gold bubbles.
A long moment with no dialogue. Just: the churn of frying oil. The soft roll of boiling
water. Wooden spoon against metal. Golden evening light thickening to amber across
the counter, catching the steam and the oil's haze like it's lit from within.
Mom watches the fillets with total attention now — nudging them gently so they don't
stick to the bottom, listening for the sound to change, the color to deepen. She lifts
one at the edge with a slotted spoon, checks the color, lowers it back.
Maya watches her mother's hands — the sureness of them, built from doing this with
less than they needed, and now stretching it further still.
MAYA
(quiet)
It smells like it used to.
Mom glances at her — just a flicker, something tender and unspoken passing between
them. She doesn't look away from the pot for long.
One by one, she lifts the fillets out, deep gold and crackling, onto a plate lined with
paper towel. The oil hisses and settles as each one comes free.
MOM
Taste this.
She tears a small corner off one fillet, blows on it, hands it to Maya. Maya takes it,
bites, and for a second just chews — eyes closing, something like relief crossing her
face.
MAYA
Perfect.
MOM
(small, satisfied)
Course it is.
They plate the food together — four bowls of spaghetti, a piece of crackling catfish laid
across each, careful that no one's portion looks smaller than another's.
They carry the bowls out toward the others — Jay, Elena, Simone waiting, low light
catching the steam rising off four plates instead of two.
Bowls set down one by one. No ceremony, just the quiet efficiency of people who've
learned to move around each other in small spaces. Maya hands Jay his plate; Elena
scoots over to make room; Simone's already reaching for a fork before hers even
lands.
For a moment, no one eats. Everyone around a table built for fewer — Mom the last to
sit, wiping her hands on her apron before finally lowering into her chair.A beat of stillness. Steam curling upward, catching the last of the amber light.
Then, without a word, they all start at once — the small clatter of forks, the first bite.
Jay closes his eyes over the fish the way Maya did earlier. He says something too
quiet to hear, and Elena laughs, soft and real.
Mom watches them eat before touching her own plate — the same look she gave
Maya earlier, multiplied across the table.
Hold on the group — heads bent over their bowls, the room lit gold, the ones who
made it this far, eating like it's nothing and like it's everything.
FINAL CONFRONTATION
EXT./INT. THE HOMESTEAD — DAY
Dre finds the building. He looks rough — hollowed out, hungry. But his eyes are still
sharp. He sees everything.
The lights. The gardens. The survivors. He sees Maya's mother alive through a
window.
He understands she knew.
DRE
How?
Maya says nothing.
DRE
How did you know?
MAYA
I had a nightmare.
DRE
A nightmare.
MAYA
The kind you wake up from different.
DRE
(quiet, not accusatory — just broken)
You could have saved us.
MAYA
I tried.
DRE
When?
MAYA
Before you became the person who needed saving.A long silence. Dre looks at the building — the life inside it. Then back at Maya.
DRE
(barely)
scared.
I was scared. I want you to know that. I was so
MAYA
I know.
DRE
Does it matter?
MAYA
(beat)
It matters that you said it.
Maya gives Dre supplies. A map. A chance. But not her sanctuary. Not her future. She
watches him go. She doesn't look away until he's gone.
ENDING

Maya stands on the rooftop. Chicago is dark. Her building glows. Plants move in the
wind. A small piece of humanity survives.
Below, she can hear voices. Her mother. Jay. Simone. Elena. People living.
MAYA (V.O.)
The first time the world ended, I lost everything.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The second time, I prepared.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
I thought being reborn meant getting revenge. I was
wrong.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
It meant I finally had the power to choose what
survived.
She looks out at the dark city. At the stars finally visible without the light pollution.
MAYA (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The nightmare showed me who we became. The
second chance showed me who we could be instead.
I chose that version. Every single day, I chose it.
FADE TO BLACK.FADE OUT.

studies.notes: - **Vector:** Bite transmission only. Airborne exposure caused initial outbreak but is now inert — survivors have passive immunity to ambient exposure, not to direct fluid contact.
The camera is a survivor too. It has limited energy, no time for elegance, and it witnesses without editorializing. Motivated camera movement only — if the camera moves, something caused it to move.

The film lives in **exhausted grief**, not active terror. The horror of the zombie apocalypse isn't the monsters — it's the weight of everything already lost. Fear is a baseline condition, not a peak event. Jump scares are cheap here; dread is the currency.
**What does surviving actually cost?**

Every survivor group is a negotiation between **individual survival instinct** and **collective survival math**. The group is safer together. The group is also the source of every interpersonal conflict, resource dispute, and moral compromise in the film. The zombie threat is external. The drama is internal.
**Studio Brain Cinematic Reference Library**

A short film is not a feature with scenes cut out. It is a **single dramatic argument** — one question, one pressure point, one emotional transaction between the audience and the film. Everything in the short exists to execute that one thing with maximum precision.
A reference guide for Studio Brain — how environments are designed to externalize theme, the director/production designer relationship, and iconic production design in cinema history.

Every location in a post-apocalyptic film carries a **before** and an **after**. The dramatic power comes from the collision between what a place was and what it is now. An abandoned hospital isn't just a dangerous location — it's a monument to the collapse of the systems that were supposed to keep people alive.
- Zombies as social commentary — consumers, soldiers, the underclass

Editing rhythm is **emotional management**. In this film, the goal is to make the audience feel the weight of survival — exhaustion, vigilance, grief — and then deploy tension against that baseline. A jump scare means nothing if the audience is already anxious. Control the baseline; control the impact.

Every survivor has a *before* — a life that shaped their skills, their damage, and their worldview. The apocalypse didn't create who they are; it stripped away everything that was concealing who they already were.
